headline: France's top book prize winner says he used AI

sources.title: Winner of the Prix Goncourt literary prize admits to using AI (The Guardian)
Goncourt 2026 winner Philippe Jaenada admits using AI in novel to 'play with reader' (Euronews)
Philippe Jaenada, lauréat du prix Goncourt, revendique un usage modéré et ludique de l'IA (Radio-Canada)

chunks.text: The winner of France's most famous book prize says he used AI in his novel. The 62-year-old French writer won on November 3, 2026. The next day, he told a French [[public radio]] station he used AI "three times." First, he {{slipped in}} one sentence written by ChatGPT as a [[playful]] game with readers. Only the prize's [[judges]] know which one. He [[joked]] that if the secret {{gets out}}, he will know who told.

verbs.wrong: To copy a line from a friend
verbs.why: She often slips in a joke at the end of her speeches. My mom slips in extra vegetables when she makes soup. The winner slipped in one sentence written by ChatGPT as a playful game with readers.

verbs.correct: To become known by other people
verbs.wrong: To be read aloud on the radio
verbs.why: Secrets get out fast in a small town. When news gets out at school, everyone talks about it. He joked that if the secret gets out, he will know who told.

chunks.text: His novel looks at the [[unsolved]] murder of a young [[artists' model]] in Paris in 1949. Second, he used AI text to [[mock]] ChatGPT's [[absurd]] answers about a [[technical detail]]. Finally, AI helped him {{look up}} facts. In his view, AI is not {{going away}}, so writers cannot pretend it does not exist. He says people must use it and [[tame]] it, but never let it {{take over}}.

verbs.correct: To find facts in a book or online
verbs.wrong: To write facts in a notebook
verbs.why: I look up new words in an online dictionary. She looks up bus times on her phone. AI helped the winner look up facts.

verbs.wrong: To get much cheaper to use
verbs.why: Some problems do not go away by themselves. This pain in my back never goes away completely. In the winner's view, AI is not going away.

verbs.correct: To take control and replace people
verbs.why: Machines take over some jobs in big factories. Weeds take over the garden when nobody cares for it. He says people must use AI but never let it take over.

chunks.text: In September 2026, the prize {{threw out}} another writer's [[first novel]] over [[suspected]] AI use. The book had {{taken off}}, selling more than 35,000 copies. A journalist checked it with a computer program that guesses if a machine wrote a text. Such programs are not always [[accurate]]. The writer {{pushed back}} and said no sentence in it was written by a machine. In October, his Canadian [[publisher]] said it found [[evidence]] of AI use and dropped him.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a contest
verbs.wrong: To read a book a second time
verbs.why: The judges throw out any photo that breaks the rules. The school throws out late entries for the art contest. In September 2026, the prize threw out another writer's first novel over suspected AI use.

verbs.wrong: To be printed in many languages
verbs.why: Some songs take off on social media in just a few days. A small cafe takes off when a famous chef praises it. The other writer's first novel had taken off, selling more than 35,000 copies.
Workers push back when the company cuts their pay. Many parents push back against new school rules. The other writer pushed back and said no sentence in his book was written by a machine.

chunks.text: The prize says it [[honors]] books "written by women and men," not machines. Readers who have {{spoken up}} online are [[divided]]. Some say AI will soon be as normal as a [[spell checker]]. Others want writers who {{come up with}} their stories by themselves. Some people {{pointed out}} that the two writers were treated differently, since only one was thrown out. Still, the winner believes AI will never write a book with "its heart, its soul, its memories."

verbs.correct: To say what you think in public
verbs.wrong: To stop reading a writer's books
verbs.why: Students speak up when a rule seems unfair. Many fans speak up online after a movie ends badly. Many readers have spoken up online about the winner's use of AI.

verbs.correct: To create a new idea or story
verbs.why: Good writers come up with fresh ideas every day. My kids come up with funny stories at bedtime. Some readers want writers who come up with their stories by themselves.

verbs.correct: To say something so others notice it
verbs.wrong: To blame a person for a mistake
verbs.why: My teacher points out my mistakes in red ink. Good friends point out when you have food on your face. Some people pointed out that the two writers were treated differently.

mainIdea.s: France's top book prize went to a novelist who later said he used AI a few times in his book. His comments came only weeks after the same prize threw out another novel over suspected AI use.
mainIdea.why: The winner says he used AI three times, once to slip in a ChatGPT sentence. In September, the prize threw out another writer's novel over suspected AI use.

mainIdea.s: The winner of a famous French book prize says a machine wrote most of his novel about a 1949 murder. He believes computers can now tell stories with just as much heart as real people.
mainIdea.why: Close, but he says he used AI only three times. He also believes AI will never write a book with heart, soul and memories.

mainIdea.s: A new study finds that people in France buy fewer printed novels each year as audiobooks grow. Bookstores in Paris have started holding free evening events to attract young readers again.
mainIdea.why: This is about a prize winner who used AI. He used it to look up facts and to slip in one ChatGPT sentence as a game.

tf.s: The winner says he slipped in one sentence written by ChatGPT.

tf.why: He told only the prize's judges. He joked that if the secret gets out, he will know who told.

tf.s: The winner believes AI is not going away.

tf.s: The other writer said a machine wrote most of his book.
tf.why: He pushed back and said no sentence in his book was written by a machine.

tf.s: The prize threw out another writer's novel over suspected AI use.
tf.why: In September 2026, the prize threw out the other writer's popular first novel.

tf.s: Everyone online agrees that using AI to write novels is fine.

lines.text: Did you hear that the winner of France's biggest book prize used AI?
Wait, didn't that same prize {{throw out}} a novel over AI in September?
It did. That's why so many people were surprised.
So how much did he use it?
Three times, he says. He {{slipped in}} one sentence from ChatGPT as a game for readers.
Only the judges know. He joked that if it {{gets out}}, he'll know who told.
Ha! Well, [[the cat's out of the bag]] about the AI, at least.
True. He also used it to {{look up}} facts for his research.
And what happened with the other writer?
His first novel had really {{taken off}}. He {{pushed back}} and said no machine wrote a word of it.
But later his publisher said it found new evidence of AI use.
Right. Some people {{pointed out}} that the two writers were treated very differently.
[[The other side of the coin]] is that the winner told everyone himself. It's all [[out in the open]].
Good point. He says AI isn't {{going away}}, but we can't let it {{take over}}.
So he thinks AI is [[here to stay]].
Yes. But for many readers, three times or thirty is [[beside the point]].
I get it. They want writers who {{come up with}} every word on their own.

expressions.expr: the cat's out of the bag
expressions.def: Used to say that a secret is now known by everyone
ex: We planned a surprise party, but the cat's out of the bag.
Once the price was posted online, the cat was out of the bag.

expressions.expr: the other side of the coin
expressions.def: Used to give the opposite view or a different way to see something
ex: The job pays well. The other side of the coin is the long hours.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is known and not hidden
ex: I'm glad our money problems are out in the open now.
Let's put all the facts out in the open.

expressions.def: Used to say that something will last and not disappear
ex: Working from home is here to stay for many people.
Electric cars are here to stay.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is not important to the main question
ex: The price is beside the point. The car is not safe.
